description: Common spelling traps, US vs UK, double letters, silent letters, 'ie/ei' rule

questions.explanation: Accommodate — one of the most commonly misspelled English words. Mnemonic: 'accommodate' has two c's, two m's, and an o between (think of 'two cottages and two motels need to accommodate guests'). Means: provide lodging or fit comfortably; adapt to. Other notorious double-letter words: occurrence (two c, two r), parallel (two l), embarrass (two r, two s), millennium (two l, two n), questionnaire (two n).

questions.stem: Which spelling is CORRECT for the verb meaning 'to get / be given'?

options.option_text: Receive (i before e EXCEPT after c)

questions.explanation: Spelling rule: 'i before e, except after c' (when the sound is 'ee'). Examples: BELIEVE, ACHIEVE, RELIEVE, GRIEF (i before e); but RECEIVE, DECEIVE, CEILING, PERCEIVE, RECEIPT (e before i, after c). Exceptions to the exception: 'weird', 'seize', 'either', 'neither' (e before i, no c), and 'science', 'efficient' (i before e, after c — but these aren't the 'ee' sound). The rule strictly applies to long 'ee' sounds.

questions.stem: The noun form of the verb 'maintain' is correctly spelled as:
questions.explanation: Maintenance — the noun from 'maintain'. Common error: people add an 'i' from the verb form, but the noun loses it. Pattern (verb → noun): maintain → maintenance, sustain → sustenance (no 'i' or 'a'), pertain → pertinence, attain → attainment (one of the few that keeps the 'a'). Other tricky -ance vs -ence words: existence (e), persistence (e), occurrence (e), independence (e), but acceptance (a), attendance (a), guidance (a). No simple rule — memorise.

questions.stem: Pick the correct spelling of the noun meaning 'a special right or advantage':
questions.explanation: Privilege — from Latin privi-legium = private law. No 'd' (a common error blends 'privilege' with 'edge'). Two i's, ends -lege. Other commonly misspelled: separate (NOT seperate; mnemonic: 'a rat in separate'); definitely (NOT definately); occasion (one s, two c — no, wait: ONE c, TWO s? actually one c, two c? — occasion has two c's no — let me recheck: o-c-c-a-s-i-o-n, two c's, one s — yes); calendar (NOT calender — calendar = the date one; calender = a roller machine).

questions.stem: Which of these is the BRITISH-English spelling (vs American)?
questions.explanation: BRITISH vs AMERICAN spelling rules: (1) -our vs -or — colour/color, favour/favor, behaviour/behavior; (2) -re vs -er — centre/center, theatre/theater, metre/meter (BUT 'meter' for the device, both); (3) -ise vs -ize — organise/organize, realise/realize (Oxford English actually uses -ize too); (4) doubled L when adding suffix — travelling/traveling, modelling/modeling, cancelled/canceled; (5) -ce vs -se nouns — defence/defense, licence (n) license (v) in UK / 'license' for both in US; (6) judgement/judgment, programme/program (program for computers in UK too). Indian English follows BRITISH conventions.

questions.stem: The verb meaning 'to make someone feel awkward or self-conscious' is spelled:
questions.explanation: Embarrass — TWO r's, TWO s's. Means: cause to feel awkward / shy / ashamed. Memory aid: 'I had to face two Rs and two Ss when I was embarrassed'. Other 'two-pair' words: harass (one r, two s — UK; or harass two r? Actually it's harass: h-a-r-a-s-s — one r, two s in standard spelling, but 'harassed' is often misspelled as 'harrassed' or 'harased'); possess (one s pair, then two more s — p-o-s-s-e-s-s — two s, then two s = four s? Let me re-check: p-o-s-s-e-s-s = 4 letters s; mnemonic: 'I will possess the success'). Spelling errors most often involve missing one of a doubled-letter pair.

questions.stem: Identify the MISSPELLED word among the following four:
questions.explanation: Definitely — derived from 'finite' → de + FINIT + ely. NOT 'definately' (a high-frequency error in writing). Other classic traps: (1) Conscience — sci in the middle ('con-SCI-ence'). (2) Liaison — l-i-a-i-s-o-n — two i's, French origin. (3) Mischievous — only THREE syllables (mis-CHIE-vous), often mispronounced as 'mis-CHIE-vi-ous' (4 syllables) and mis-spelled as 'mischievious'. (4) Pronunciation — pro-nun-CI-A-tion (NOT 'pronounciation'). (5) Restaurant — restau-RANT (with -au-, French loanword).
